starterQuestions.q: Explain what is meant by 'semiconservative replication' of DNA.
starterQuestions.a: Each newly synthesized DNA molecule contains one original (template) parental strand and one newly formed daughter strand.

starterQuestions.q: Describe the function of the enzyme DNA Helicase at the replication fork.
starterQuestions.a: Unwinds and separates the parental double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.

starterQuestions.q: Define an mRNA 'codon' and explain how a triplet of bases codes for an amino acid.
starterQuestions.a: A sequence of 3 mRNA nucleotides that codes for a specific amino acid or stop signal according to the genetic code.

starterQuestions.q: Describe the role of RNA Polymerase during the transcription of a gene.
starterQuestions.a: Binds promoter, unwinds DNA, and synthesizes single-stranded pre-mRNA 5' to 3' using complementary RNA nucleotides.

starterQuestions.q: Identify molecule 'X' shown in the diagram and state its primary role in translation.
starterQuestions.a: Transfer RNA (tRNA); delivers its specific amino acid to the ribosome matching its anticodon to the complementary mRNA codon.

starterQuestions.q: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being 'degenerate' and 'non-overlapping'.
starterQuestions.a: Degenerate: multiple codons encode the same amino acid. Non-overlapping: each base is read in only one triplet frame.

courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology - Unit F172: Genetics
focus: Acquired vs Inherited Mutations, Mutational Mechanisms & Huntington's CAG Repeat Pathology
deliverable: Classify somatic acquired vs germline inherited mutations with concrete examples, contrast molecular mutation types (missense, nonsense, frameshift), and analyze the molecular pathology, CAG repeat thresholds, anticipation, and autosomal dominant transmission of Huntington's disease.

objectives.knowledge: Distinguish between acquired (somatic) and inherited (germline) mutations, classifying point mutations (missense, nonsense, silent) and indels.
objectives.application: Explain the molecular mechanism of CAG triplet repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4p16.3 and interpret clinical repeat thresholds (<26, 27-35, 36-39, >=40).
objectives.evaluation: Evaluate the relationship between polyglutamine tract length, genetic anticipation (especially paternal transmission), striatal neurodegeneration, and autosomal dominant inheritance.

terminology.def: Somatic: acquired non-heritable mutations in body tissues driving cancer. Germline: mutations in sperm/egg passed to offspring.
A tandem repetition of Cytosine-Adenine-Guanine in exon 1 of the HTT gene encoding an expanded polyglutamine (polyQ) tract.
Alleles with 40 or more CAG repeats confer a 100% lifetime probability of developing Huntington's disease.
Progression towards earlier age of onset and increased symptom severity across generations due to meiotic repeat expansion during gametogenesis.
Misfolded mutant huntingtin protein aggregating into toxic inclusion bodies that destroy striatal GABAergic neurons in the basal ganglia.

theoryPoints: Inheritance Boundary: Somatic mutations (e.g. UV skin damage) cannot be inherited because somatic lineages do not contribute genetic material to gametes.
CAG Repeat Expansion Scale: Normal <=26; Intermediate 27–35 (unaffected, but mutable); Reduced penetrance 36–39; Full penetrance >=40 (inverse correlation with age of onset).

Paternal Anticipation Bias: Instability and slippage of DNA polymerase during the thousands of mitotic/meiotic divisions of spermatogenesis cause greater repeat expansion through paternal transmission.
Autosomal Dominant Risk: A single mutant HTT allele is sufficient to cause pathology; each child of an affected heterozygous parent faces a 50% risk.

workedExample.title: Huntington's Diagnostic CAG Repeat & Pedigree Anticipation
workedExample.subtitle: Analyzing triplet repeat lengths and inheritance risk across three generations

steps.label: Step 1: Paternal Grandfather
steps.detail: Carried an intermediate allele of 33 CAG repeats (unaffected, normal lifespan). During spermatogenesis, DNA replication slippage expanded the repeat tract.

steps.label: Step 2: Affected Father
steps.detail: Inherited 42 CAG repeats (full penetrance). Developed classic motor chorea and cognitive changes at age 48 (autosomal dominant Hh).

steps.label: Step 3: Offspring Transmission
steps.detail: During father's spermatogenesis, further expansion occurred to 54 CAG repeats in his child.

steps.label: Step 4: Clinical Anticipation Outcome
steps.detail: The child experiences onset of juvenile Huntington's disease in their late teens (~18 years), demonstrating genetic anticipation with earlier onset and increased severity.

hingeQuestions.question: A 32-year-old individual undergoes predictive genetic testing for Huntington's disease and is found to have 44 CAG repeats on one allele of the HTT gene. How should this result be interpreted?
options: Normal allele; the individual will never develop the condition
Intermediate carrier; individual is unaffected but offspring are at risk
Full penetrance allele; the individual will develop Huntington's disease if they live a normal lifespan, and each child has a 50% risk
Recessive carrier; disease will only develop if the spouse also carries the allele
hingeQuestions.explanation: Alleles with >=40 CAG repeats have 100% full penetrance for Huntington's disease, and as an autosomal dominant trait, each child has a 50% risk of inheritance.

hingeQuestions.question: Why do somatic mutations in the TP53 gene in skin cancer cells fail to pass to the patient's biological children?
options: Somatic mutations are automatically repaired during embryonic development
Somatic cells do not form gametes; only germline mutations in sperm or ova are transmissible to offspring
TP53 is only present in somatic tissue
Maternal mitochondrial DNA suppresses paternal mutations
hingeQuestions.explanation: Somatic mutations are confined to non-reproductive differentiated cell lineages and never enter meiotic germ cells or gametes.

hingeQuestions.question: What molecular mechanism is directly responsible for genetic anticipation in Huntington's disease families?
options: Progressive methylation of the promoter over time
DNA polymerase replication slippage during gametogenesis (especially spermatogenesis) adding further CAG repeats across generations
Accumulation of point mutations in mitochondrial DNA
hingeQuestions.explanation: Replication slippage during meiosis expands the unstable CAG repeat sequence, leading to longer polyglutamine tracts and earlier onset in successive generations.

examQuestion.question: Explain the difference between acquired somatic mutations and inherited germline mutations, and analyze how a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene causes Huntington's disease, explaining the phenomenon of genetic anticipation. [6 marks]
guidance: Somatic vs Germline Distinction: Somatic mutations occur in non-gamete body tissues and cannot be passed to offspring (driving cancer); germline mutations arise in gametes and are inherited by all cells of offspring [2 marks].

CAG Repeat Molecular Pathology: Unstable CAG expansion in HTT gene (exon 1, chromosome 4p16.3) encodes an elongated polyglutamine tract; >=40 repeats confers full penetrance; toxic gain-of-function mutant protein aggregates and causes selective neurodegeneration in striatal medium spiny neurons of the basal ganglia [2 marks].

Genetic Anticipation Mechanism: DNA replication slippage during meiosis (particularly paternal transmission during spermatogenesis) further expands repeat length, resulting in earlier age of onset and increased symptom severity across generations [2 marks].

plenary: Mutations are classified by origin (somatic vs germline) and molecular type (substitutions vs frameshifts).
Huntington's disease is an exemplar triplet repeat disorder (CAG >=40 causes full-penetrance neurodegeneration).
Genetic anticipation is driven by meiotic repeat expansion during gametogenesis.
Next Lesson: Pedigree chart analysis & inheritance risk calculations — decoding family trees and computing precise genetic probabilities.
